the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the pesticides directive and the pesticide regulation are properly implemented. parliament has rightly insisted on legislation that is both effective and appropriate to the problems. there has been a parliamentary dialectic, but above all there has been strong resistance in the council and there have been economic powers which have been strongly mobilized in defence of preconstituted interests. we must look instead to the general interest: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's agricultural policy is not affected by the effects of the pesticides used in the production of foodstuffs. there's an overuse of chemicals in agriculture that's hurting everyone: the food, the environment, the farmers who have to pay dearly for these industrial products. the misuse of chemicals is linked to an old model, that of agriculture based on quantity rather than quality, in which products are separated by territories, seasons and work, a model which is costly for everyone, a model which is also harmful because of its impact on the greenhouse effect. these regulations which we approve must therefore be incorporated in the construction of a healthier and more modern model of quality agriculture which is useful to the citizens and the environment with more work and more income. i must say that our work has produced positive results. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the objective of reducing the presence of pesticides, and not just their hazardous nature, has only been included among the commitments to be achieved in the respective national plans, especially for high-risk substances. if priority should therefore be given to non-chemical methods, to the protection and integrity of soil and water resources, avoiding any contamination of a common good such as water, then these individual countries must have a sense of this great responsibility in reducing the sustainable use of pesticides. aerial spraying is prohibited and where there are no objective alternatives the composition, timing, intensity and times must be notified to the population in advance. progress has also been made in the area of the right to information and access to data on the internet. we would have liked to see the idea of three rigid zones dropped from the regulation, but it was retained by the council. the results are important, however, and measures will be taken to combat the smuggling of illegal, counterfeit and dangerous substances, and others alongside these. we are making a good step forward and i hope that the vote in parliament will not lead to any negative consequences!

member of the commission. − madam president, first of all i would like to convey the regrets of vice-president tajani for not being with us. he is on a very important mission to japan. let me go straight to the point. the commission remains fully committed to developing an eu policy in the field of urban mobility because it is convinced that, although responsibilities for urban mobility lie primarily with local, regional and national authorities, in some specific areas there is an added value of action at european level. as a matter of fact, although cities are all different, they face common challenges. the problems in urban mobility are significant and growing and affect many citizens and businesses, which are confronted with traffic safety problems, with limited accessibility of public transport, with congestion and health problems caused by pollution. to illustrate the importance of urban mobility, let me provide you with some figures: 60% of the population lives in urban areas and 85% of the eu gdp is created there. however, cities also generate 40% of co2 emissions, and two out of three road accidents take place in urban areas. finally, congestion, which is one of the main problems that citizens have to face everyday, is responsible for the loss of about 1% of the eu’s gdp every year. sustainable urban mobility is therefore a key element to achieve our goals with respect to climate change, economic growth and road safety. this is why the commission has been launching actions in this field since 1995, in order to promote the exchange of best practices. the highlight has been the extremely successful civitas programme that started in 2000. the 2007 green paper ‘towards a new culture in urban mobility’ then identified broad areas for potential complementary action at eu level to promote greener and safer cities and smarter and accessible urban transport. but what can be done concretely at eu level? we can help local authorities to implement related eu policies and to make best use of eu funding. eu-wide dissemination and replication of innovative approaches can give authorities the possibility to achieve more and better results at lower cost. we can help foster markets for new technologies, for example clean and energy-efficient vehicles, and facilitate harmonised standards for broad market introduction of new technologies. finally, the eu can guide authorities towards solutions that are interoperable and facilitate smoother functioning of the single market. the commission will therefore continue to act, because we think, as a large majority of stakeholders do, that there is much to be gained from working at eu level to support initiatives at the local, regional and national levels. now let me answer your question: why the adoption of the action plan on urban mobility has been delayed. unfortunately, the conditions were not appropriate for the adoption of a comprehensive action plan by the commission before the end of 2008. but my colleague vice-president tajani would like to reassure you that he remains committed to working towards the adoption of the action plan and to develop an eu policy in the field of urban transport in full respect of the subsidiarity and proportionality principles. to this purpose, it is not the intention of the commission to propose a one-size-fits-all solution; on the contrary, we would like to develop a toolbox, including short- and medium-term practical actions, in order to provide cities with the tools to address, in an integrated way, specific issues related to urban mobility. then, it will be up to local authorities to decide what is more suitable for them, according to their own objectives and needs. in order to address the concerns that might still exist regarding the strategic role of the eu in urban mobility, vice-president tajani’s intention is to demonstrate with concrete actions how the eu can add value and quality to urban mobility in europe. on the basis of the responses to the green paper and many discussions with stakeholders, a number of actions have been identified and will be launched later this year. to promote innovative solutions and new technologies, we have already opened a call for proposals, closing at the end of march, which will provide up to 50% funding to the projects selected. once the directive on the promotion of clean and energy efficient road transport vehicles comes into force, around march, we will initiate the development of an internet site to facilitate joint clean vehicle procurement. on information and exchange of approaches, we intend to start up, around april, a website providing information on urban mobility legislation and funding in europe, as well as on good practice. we will also reflect with stakeholders on the future of our civitas programme and how to build on the vast knowledge and experience generated in the civitas-funded actions. finally, to help increasing knowledge on sustainable mobility policies, we will launch a study on aspects related to green zones and a study on the opportunities for making public transport systems more interoperable. we intend also to establish an expert network for considering aspects of urban road pricing and internalisation of external costs. i am convinced that this package of actions, which will be soon undertaken at eu level, provides an important basis for moving forward in the field of urban mobility.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, exactly one year ago we decided to combine the reports on public finances for 2007 and 2008. there were at least two reasons: the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the situation in the community. the intensity of the changes was not yet known, but it was already clear that analysing the two years together would allow us to make a more complete and adequate analysis. nothing could be further from the truth. the report we are voting on tomorrow has been updated constantly. the very close link between public finances and the financial and economic crisis is clear. it is enough to think of the allocation of resources for the rescue of banks and businesses, the support of the production system, taking into account the demand coming mainly from small and mediumsized enterprises, and protection against the negative effects of the recession for citizens. all these measures are the concern of the european institutions and individual member states, but they should not undermine or weaken the prospects and our commitment to future generations. the report shall cover at least two areas: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. the principle that quality and sustainable public finances are indispensable not for individual countries but for the survival of the european economy and social model is confirmed, indeed reinforced. as regards income, the tax base must be extended without weakening the principle of progressivity and the tax burden on labour must be reduced, especially for low- and middle-income earners and for pensions. as regards expenditure, the context, needs and composition of the population must be assessed, with attention to gender policies and demographic changes. rather than cutting indiscriminately, we need to restructure expenditure, reallocate budgetary items and modernise public administrations. a useful methodology is gender budgeting, which has long been wanted and promoted by the european parliament, but is still far from becoming commonly used, although it allows for greater transparency, comparability, awareness by the public and thus increases trust and a sense of responsibility. unprecedented instability must be dealt with firmly. if public sector intervention is to become central and essential again, it is essential to avoid repeating mistakes that would be even more unforgivable and to turn the crisis towards a new model of development that is truly environmentally and socially sustainable. when we talk about coordination at european level, we must think about having our own governance in a counter-cyclical function and with shared and unidirectional commitments, strengthening the fight against tax evasion and tax havens and linking up national plans. in the case of business support measures, the impact on competition, the functioning of the internal market and the level playing field must be assessed, and supervision, accountability, limitations and consequential behaviour must be ensured. the revision of the stability and growth pact allows for controlled flexibility, to be used with care and foresight. the common macroeconomic policies and investments in the strategic areas that have been defined in advance must be reinvigorated, with instruments such as eurobonds and with great attention also paid to subnational and regional stability plans. the report was widely supported in the committee on economic and monetary affairs, as most of the political groups agreed with this view. i hope this is a prelude to a good outcome of the vote tomorrow!

on behalf of the uen group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, after ten years the growing role of the euro in international trade and its use as a reserve currency show that it is the world's currency of reference, that it has guaranteed monetary stability and contributed to the integration of the economies of the states which have adopted it, despite some errors of assessment which have created problems for citizens both in terms of the real exchange value between the national currency and the euro and in terms of the few checks carried out on the costs of goods and services. the euro was born without external impositions, without wars of conquest or political hegemony. it was the result of the free convergence of eleven governments, who believed in the creation of economic and monetary union, as provided for in the treaties and as an essential step in trying to achieve that political union which, unfortunately, is still a goal to be achieved. some of the problems that have occurred are due to the inefficiency of a system that had not foreseen the ways to drive the other major concomitant phenomenon, namely the acceleration of the process of globalization and the major changes in the reasons for trade at the international level. the euro has helped us to cope with a number of difficulties, the most serious of which was the current financial crisis, and it has protected us from the severe tensions that have arisen on the markets. if we had not had the euro, we would have had a worse experience than in 1992. on this 10th anniversary, we welcome the entry of slovakia, the 16th country to join the euro area. the measures taken by the ecb and the commission to deal with the current crisis have played a buffer and a containment role, but we continue to maintain, as we have done on several occasions in this house, that we consider it inconceivable to have a monetary policy that is independent of economic policy. it is true that the real situation is a bit anomalous: 16 countries with a single currency, 27 national political economies, coordinated as far as possible by the commission, and 11 countries with national currencies. coordinating monetary policy with an economic policy which does not in fact exist is certainly not an easy task, but if the institutions responsible for the economic policies of our countries do not engage in dialogue with the central banks and the ecb, which sums them up and vice versa, the european union will find it increasingly difficult to deal jointly not only with the current crisis but also with the continuing challenges that the outside world and globalisation bring us at home. we hope that recent experience will convince us of the need to face change in europe, by bringing the real economy back to the centre and by bringing greater cohesion and connection between the central bank and the european institutions responsible for policy and programme direction. the very recent energy crisis has also shown that a common economic policy on the major strategic issues is of vital interest to the citizens and cannot be postponed, and that if there is political will its birth is facilitated precisely by the increasingly evident weight of the euro.

member of the commission. - mr president, madam member, ladies and gentlemen, fisheries are by their very nature the most globalised of the professions and are facing globalisation in all its fullness. it is estimated that some 30 million workers are employed in this sector, and these people are exposed to considerable hardship and danger in addition to the effects of globalization. a comparison of the number of fatalities in the fishing industry with the rate of fatalities at work in general, according to the international labour organisation statistics, shows that fishing is one of the most risky professions in the world. all the european institutions support a widely recognised decent work programme. the commission has recently reinforced its commitment with a renewed social agenda and report following up on the 2006 decent work communication. an important part of the commission's approach is to promote international labour standards. the general improvement of safety, medical and legal protection in the fisheries sector and the approximation of the level of social protection enjoyed by other workers can only be achieved if efforts are made to establish minimum standards at global level. the eu member states, as members of the international labour organisation, have contributed within their means and with the support of the commission to the development of an updated and comprehensive convention setting out such international minimum standards, complemented by compliance mechanisms and enforcement mechanisms such as inspections in foreign ports subject to certain conditions. together with a non-legally binding recommendation, the convention was adopted by the highest body of the international labour organisation in june 2007. convention 188 revises several older ilo standards relating to fishermen and its entry into force could create a level playing field and a better environment for all. the convention regulates such matters as minimum age, medical examinations, crew placement, rest periods, employment contracts, repatriation, recruitment and placement of workers, pay, accommodation and food, medical care and social security. parts of the new convention relate to the coordination of social security, an area of exclusive community competence. the council must therefore authorise the member states to ratify those parts. several other topics are also covered by the area of shared competence. given that the new international labour organisation standard must take effect as soon as possible, the commission proposes that the convention should include a call on member states to seek the deposit of their instruments of ratification as soon as possible, preferably by 21 december 2012. this call will be supported by a review of the ratification situation by the council by january 2012.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fisheries sector is not left to the detriment of the environment. it is therefore a sector which requires extensive regulation and comprehensive international standards to ensure adequate protection of the living and working conditions of fishermen throughout the world, who are often exposed to serious exploitation situations. the convention 188 on labour in fisheries is therefore a key piece of legislation, designed to establish equal conditions of organization in the sector and fairer conditions of competition. as has been said, it promotes decent living and working conditions for fishermen, health and safety at work, adequate rest periods, the composition of the crew list, repatriation, recruitment, wages and social security. we would therefore - and this first debate has also shown how much we agree on the importance of this measure - simply stress the need and urgency of its ratification by the member states so that it can be considered as coming into force as soon as possible.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we are starting from a concept: the mediterranean diet, as confirmed by numerous studies, is a good way to combat obesity and cardiovascular disease and is generally very good for human health in many ways. but the point here is not to try to impose the mediterranean diet on the whole of the eu or to try to favour it over other diets that are better adapted to climates and regions other than the mediterranean. but we have a duty to protect it, to define it in its content and its characteristics, to defend it against external imitations and contamination which could damage its image and value. it must therefore be valued, like all other european cultural expressions that deserve to be defended and promoted at global level. it is a model which the world is trying to copy and it is therefore important to specify its peculiarities and safeguard it, to avoid an entirely european heritage being lost in the sea of globalisation.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking my colleagues for the excellent cooperation which has enabled us to draw up a very satisfactory text. i would also like to thank all the ngos and institutions which have followed our work closely and have enriched the report with valuable suggestions. two main objectives have been pursued in our work. first of all: closely monitor the state of implementation of the 2003 framework decision within the 27 member states. the second objective was to propose necessary improvements. the framework decision needs to be updated to raise the threshold for the protection of minors, taking into account the spread of new and worrying exploitation phenomena, also linked to new technologies. the fight against sex tourism is one of our priorities. this is a worryingly growing phenomenon, linked also to the fall in travel costs. in this context, it is necessary to improve extraterritorial cooperation and to ask the member states to exclude the principle of double criminalization for crimes related to the exploitation and abuse of children. secondly: it is necessary that grooming, i.e. psychological manipulation of a child online for sexual purposes, should be considered a criminal offence in all member states. thirdly: we need to bind member states to the obligation to exchange information contained in criminal records relating to final convictions for sexual abuse offences. the aim is to exclude the possibility of sexual abusers from working in a profession which involves contact with minors. among the proposals to be implemented as soon as possible is the launch of the rapid alert system for missing children. it is a system which has already been tried and tested, and which has already been put into practice, albeit by a small number of member states and therefore only on an experimental basis, but which has achieved excellent results. and so there is a need to make it operational in all 27 member states. it is worth remembering that every year thousands and thousands of children are lost in europe. i would like to stress one more point. in general, national the rapporteur. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, four minutes will suffice to sum up two years of work, laborious but i believe useful work, which has seen parliament, the commission with its proposal and the council, work which has the merit of proposing, for the first time with this directive, sanctions for employers who exploit the work of illegal immigrants. i think we have succeeded in reversing some of the logic behind this directive, which was limited to the fight against illegal immigration. the compromise text with the council also provides protection for those immigrants who are forced to work underground, often as hostages of mafia crime. the risk, madam president, of otherwise being punished twice, as exploited workers, often forced to accept unfair working conditions, and as irregular workers, forced to be repatriated, with a ban on repatriation which, in many countries, means years and years. in this connection, we have provided in articles 7 and 14 that in cases involving minors, cases of serious exploitation and trafficking in human beings, member states must provide for rules for the issue of temporary residence permits, the duration of which may be extended until the arrears are paid. we would have liked to have extended this possibility to all illegal immigrants, but we are prevented from doing so by the return directive, which was adopted last year and the speaker is not one of those who supported it. we have, however, succeeded in introducing a rule which allows member states to apply more favourable measures to immigrants in the matter of issuing residence permits. article 10 - i believe it is the key article - imposes for the first time penal sanctions in the most serious cases, including the case where regular workers are minors. the secondary sanctions provided for in article 8 are important, i think: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full, and irregular migrant to the wage of a regular worker, without any discrimination. we have included in the scope of the directive temporary agencies which, especially in some countries, including my own, are the organizations most easily engaged in recruiting illegal labour in conditions of absolute and extreme exploitation. think of the cases of corporal's murder that have long been covered in the black press. we have asked and gotten unions to represent immigrants in administrative and civil cases. the text used to refer to third parties in general terms, but now it refers to trade unions. a period of inquiry is needed, and that is why we have asked the commission, three years after the directive enters into force, to report to parliament and the council specifically on the rules concerning inspections, residence permits, penalties and subcontracting. the rapporteur would like to extend responsibility to the whole procurement chain as originally envisaged by the commission. the council and parliament, and partly part of parliament, were about to exclude subcontracting altogether; we have come to a compromise solution which i think is useful: the commission has already the compromise we are going to vote a statement that the provisions of article 9 do not prejudice future legislative measures on subcontracting. in conclusion, madam president, i believe that this directive speaks to us of a europe in which immigration finally becomes a matter of collective responsibility and recognized rights, not just of rules against immigrants.
the commission has said that there are between 4.5 and 8 million non-eu citizens in europe who are in an irregular situation. it's a completely irrelevant phenomenon. the european union is a global economy. it's obviously an over-amplified phenomenon. these are workers who provide useful services, personal services, work in the tourism sector and are absorbed in the vast majority of cases by the labour market. they are workers who are useful to our economy, but they are exploited workers, exploited to lower the cost of labour, to enrich unscrupulous employers, they are workers who often perform activities which are not covered by the citizens of the european union. we need these people, but these people have entered irregularly for a simple reason, because there is no way in europe to enter regularly, as there is for the vast majority of citizens who are now in regular status and who entered the european union irregularly. we need another measure, a measure to regularize these millions of people, a measure to free them from slavery, from blackmail, from exploitation. instead, we are dealing with a directive which marks the continuation of the return directive. we have decided on the method of expulsion, and today we are deciding on the potential pool of expulsions and also on who is paying for the expulsions. the exploited under this directive pay more than the exploiter. unfortunately, there is no provision for a general regularization measure for those who denounce their status, for those who denounce the exploiter, for those who denounce the crime that is being committed. you go from blackmailing a black job straight to expulsion. we needed something else, we needed a measure that would promote legality, not the criminalization of those who are currently in a state of irregularity. we needed a measure to stem xenophobia. the italian minister for the interior said yesterday that "we must be bad with illegal immigrants", that we must be bad with those who are in a vulnerable situation. i believe that this directive is encouraging these xenophobic attitudes. we in the european union need migrants says the commission: 50 million by 2060 because we are in the midst of a demographic crisis, but we are doing nothing to bring them in, we are harmonizing the system of expulsions and today we are deciding to expel those who are in an irregular situation despite being a worker absorbed by the european labour market. i believe that the effects of this directive will be devastating because they will serve to increase the clandestinity of migrants, the flooding of the labour market and will increase the blackmailing crimes of unscrupulous employers.

flows more efficiently. all parties stand to gain by such an approach. the development and shaping of an eu asylum and migration policy depends on your input too. i am grateful to parliament for its positive contribution and i am sure that we can work constructively on further developing this important policy area. you have specifically raised the situation on the islands of mayotte and lampedusa. we should take care to distinguish between the two types of migratory flows in these two cases. the migratory flows affecting lampedusa and mayotte can be characterised as mixed ones: some of the third-country nationals concerned have claimed international protection, others certainly fall into the category of economic immigrants. regarding the first category – those who claim international protection – i would draw your attention to the existence of minimum standards for the protection of asylum seekers, set out in directive 2003/9/ec, which was adopted in 2003. this directive has already been transposed into the national law of the member states and it is for the commission to ensure that the provisions set out in this directive are properly and fully applied. in december 2008, the commission presented to the european parliament and to the council a proposal to amend and update this directive. since the codecision procedure applies here, the european parliament will be fully involved in the negotiations on this new proposal. the council will shortly begin consideration of this new proposal and looks forward to working closely with you. honourable members will be aware that, in the specific case of the french overseas territory of mayotte, community law does not apply. with regard to the second category – other third-country nationals who have unlawfully entered the territory of a member state – the competent authorities of the member states are entitled to detain those falling in this category prior to the adoption of a return decision, and/or with a view to facilitating its enforcement. detention may prove to be the only option in cases where it is necessary to seek identification of third-country nationals without travel documents. until now, the legislation and practice regarding detention in the member states has varied considerably. the recently adopted european parliament and council directive on common standards and procedures for returning illegally staying third-country nationals has introduced specific principles and rules on detention, and so goes some way to establishing a common legal framework in this area. this directive clearly states that detention for the purposes of removal may be used only where less coercive measures cannot be applied in a particular case and only on specific, very limited grounds. furthermore, the directive provides that detention shall be for as short a period as possible, shall require a decision in writing with reasons in fact and law, and shall be subject to judicial review at regular intervals. it should also be stressed that the directive provides for clear upper limits of detention and the grounds on which – in limited specific cases – a detention period may be prolonged, but not longer than a maximum term. on the conditions of detention, the directive makes clear that detention shall take place as a rule in specialised detention facilities – or, in any case, away from ordinary prisoners – and that the rights of the detainees – especially those of vulnerable status including minors and families – shall be observed. as far as the return of illegal immigrants is concerned, the recently adopted european parliament and council directive on common standards and procedures for returning illegally staying third-country nationals is already in force. its provisions now have to be transposed by member states into their national law within a deadline of two years. this overall legal framework underlines our strong commitment to ensuring that third-country nationals who are held in detention for the purpose of removal are treated in a humane and dignified manner, and that their fundamental rights are fully respected. it also, through the most recent legislation, sets commonly agreed standards on return policy. this framework is not only in line with the principles i set out at the beginning of my statement, but actually gives them legal force. our asylum and migration policy is thus rooted in the rule of law. it ensures respect for human rights and for the dignity of the individual.
the commission's vice-president - mr president, as the president-in-office of the council, mr vondra, has just said, we now have a legal framework which is beginning to take hold. the first step is the return directive, which is the first horizontal act to harmonise the standards in the member states on return. it introduces into community law the applicable provisions of the european convention on human rights and its implementation will allow the application of community control mechanisms to monitor compliance with the acquis. i am well aware that this directive may have been considered by some of you at times as insufficient. it is nevertheless a means of community control which allows us to check that the acquis is being respected. of course, by monitoring its implementation - i remind you that the transposition period is until 24 december 2010 - the commission will ensure that the fundamental principles of respect for the rights of migrants are strictly observed and will assess, in particular, the impact of the detention provisions. i myself have said that i would be following the transposition closely so that some member states do not use it as a pretext for extending the period of detention they currently observe. others, for whom detention was indefinite, will be required to comply with the time limit laid down in the directive. the second text we will be using is the one adopted by the college on 3 december 2008 on the reception conditions for asylum seekers. i hope, mr president, that the libe committee will be able to examine this text in the near future, which will allow us to make progress in this new asylum policy. i would remind you that this text contains clear rules on detention, in full compliance with fundamental rights, and limits detention to exceptional cases - this is the case for asylum seekers, we agree. secondly, it better takes into account the needs of vulnerable asylum seekers and it will also facilitate access to the labour market for asylum seekers. so we now have a legal framework and we obviously need to use it. i now come to the questions which parliament has sought to raise in this debate. the commission is aware of the difficult situation facing the italian authorities due to the massive arrivals of irregular migrants and asylum seekers on the southern coasts of the country, in particular in lampedusa. so far italy has managed to grant access to its territory, saving the lives of many migrants and establishing a procedure to process asylum applications under good conditions. the commission notes that italy has acknowledged the need for international protection in half of the individual cases, which further demonstrates that these flows include both asylum seekers and, of course, irregular immigrants. for several years now, the commission has been providing financial resources, in particular to support certain member states, including italy. this was the case with the præsidium project or the emergency measures of the european refugee fund. and a few weeks ago the commission approved emergency aid of €7 million. if italy deems it necessary, the commission is ready to consider a new request for emergency assistance under the 2009 budget in order to improve reception facilities both in lampedusa and in sicily and on the mainland, and thus to strengthen the capacity of the italian authorities to examine the individual situations of migrants in good conditions. i myself will be going to lampedusa very soon, as i will also be going to malta, to look at the situation there. i am also very aware that one of the keys to the solution lies in establishing a strong framework of cooperation with libya, the main transit country on east african migration routes. and i support the efforts of my colleague, mrs benita ferrero-waldner, to achieve a rapid result in the current negotiations. it is one of the keys, and without this negotiation and its outcome it will be very difficult to deal with all the problems that have arisen. i'm going to mayotte. the return directive contains specific rules on detention conditions, with particular emphasis on minors and families, but these community rules do not apply to the territory of mayotte for the time being. the european union recognises the territory of mayotte as french but with the status of an overseas country and territory, not as an outermost region. so private law does not apply, but it is a fact that france must take account of the indications and requests of the council of europe and i believe that the french authorities are considering other conditions for reception in mayotte. it is true, however, that european law is not directly applicable, because union law is not directly applicable in a territory which is not an outermost region. these are the few indications i wanted to give when i told you and reiterated to parliament how much i am concerned about the reception conditions of irregular immigrants, and a fortiori asylum seekers, and how much they are a priority for me. that is why i am going to make these trips to see how things are going in the field. i am grateful to parliament for having opened this debate.

the agenda includes statements by the council and the commission on the impact of the financial crisis on the automobile industry.
president-in-office of the council. − mr president, i think that we are now moving into a really important issue. under the current circumstances, this is something that must be discussed. once again, we are grateful for this timely opportunity to discuss the effect of the current economic and financial crisis on the automobile industry. as many of you are following very closely in your constituencies, the automobile industry is a key factor for the whole of the european economy. over the years, we have promoted the competitiveness of the sector by establishing a single european automobile market and calling for fairer competition in trade with third countries. more recently, we have focused on reducing car emissions in order to combat air pollution and climate change. in all these areas this parliament has given us its consistent support. thanks to these efforts, and in particular to the resilience and adaptability of the european automobile industry, european cars are today among the best, the most innovative and the most competitive, as well as the safest, most fuel-efficient and environmentally sustainable in the world. we should be proud of europe’s record. nevertheless, despite its resilience, and as a result of factors largely outside its control, the european automotive sector has been particularly badly hit by the global economic crisis. these difficulties were already apparent in november last year, when the council agreed on an approach based on promoting even more sustainable and fuel-efficient cars, realistic targets for manufacturers, and effective incentives for stimulating demand. in the short time since then, the situation has become more serious. the industry has reported that 8% fewer cars were sold in the union last year than in the previous year, to compare 2008 with 2007. the situation is likely to remain as bad – if it does not get worse – in 2009, hitting not just the automotive constructors, but also the whole automotive industry supply chain. ministers met my friend, günter verheugen, the commissioner and the vice-president of the commission, on 16 january to discuss the specific problems facing the automobile industry. they expressed particular concern that the current difficulties would put at risk a significant number of jobs and underlined the importance they attached to the future of the industry. of course, the primary responsibility for responding to these challenges rests with the industry itself. the industry must be encouraged to take all necessary steps to address structural problems such as overcapacity and lack of investment in new technologies. however, the importance of this industry for the european economy, and the fact that the sector is hit particularly hard by the current crisis, means that some sort of public support is required. this is reflected in the european economic recovery plan agreed by the european council last december, as well as in the member states’ national programmes. of course, we cannot allow short-term support for the industry to undermine its long-term competitiveness. this means focusing clearly on innovation. member states agree that public support for the automotive industry needs to be both targeted and coordinated. it also needs to respect some key principles, such as fair competition and open markets. it should not be about a race for subsidies, and it should not result in market distortions. in order to achieve this, member states have confirmed their willingness to cooperate closely with the commission on both supply-side and demand-side measures taken nationally. the commission has, in turn, undertaken to provide a swift response in cases where it is required to react. more generally, the council’s presidency fully supports the commission on the need to advance rapidly with the implementation of the european economic recovery plan. the commission has also been invited to explore, together with the european investment bank, how the utilisation of the loans envisaged for this sector can be further improved in terms of rapid availability, project financing and frontloading of the loans, without discriminating between manufacturers and member states. with regard to the global environment, we clearly need to engage in an early dialogue with the new us administration as well as with our other global partners. the czech presidency is determined to push forward with this overall policy of support for the industry, whilst respecting the principles and parameters to which i have referred. there is already a wide range of community instruments which can play their part in providing support, not least in the area of new technology, for example in the development of clean cars. the full potential of innovative and environmentally sustainable propulsion technologies – fuel cells, hybrid, electrical, solar power – needs to be fully explored and put into operation. on the other hand, there are also more ready-made and rapidly available instruments, such as, for example, the scrapping scheme for old cars. these instruments could combine the demand impulse for new cars with positive externalities in terms of transport security, reduction of emissions and others. there are now several member states which already use this instrument. therefore, the presidency would like to ask the commission immediately to put forward a proposal on how to encourage, in a coordinated manner, european car fleet renewal in the area of vehicle recovery and recycling, based on the analysis of the impact of these schemes in different member states. our aim is to have a proposal from the commission some time ahead of the spring european council, in the context of the evaluation of the recovery plan, and to be able to discuss the issue during the competitiveness council in march. this will be headed by my colleague martin říman and vice-president of the commission, günter verheugen. such schemes may provide an important demand stimulus for the automotive industry at community level and should also ensure a level playing field within the internal market. i would like to underline the second half of the sentence, also in the current context. to summarise: this is not just about supporting a key sector of our economy but is an approach from which we all stand to benefit in the long run.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, the european council has been a very important meeting. mr alexandr vondra has just told you what came out of the meeting i held with the ministers responsible for the motor vehicle industry on 16 january. i can only confirm all this, but i would still advise caution. we must also be careful not to create expectations or hopes that we cannot possibly fulfill. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. cars are an early indicator of economic development. it was therefore not surprising that the severe drop in demand for cars, which we experienced from last summer, was followed by a downturn in all other economic sectors. why is that? the decline in demand is an expression of a lack of confidence in economic development. consumers behave no differently from businesses. in uncertain economic times, when you don't know what's coming, you keep your money together. in the private household, the purchase of a new car over several years is the largest investment. it can be postponed, however, because a european car can still be driven for another year. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. that is why the measures we are taking together in europe to combat the crisis as a whole are of the utmost importance. i want to give you a few more figures to help you understand the meaning: the european automotive industry directly and indirectly employs 12 million people, or 6% of all jobs in the european union. it is the most important economic sector for our exports. the biggest export surplus we ever make is on cars. we produced 19.6 million cars in europe in 2007, almost a million fewer last year and this year it will decrease again significantly. there are about 2 million unsold cars on hold right now. the automotive industry is the industry with the highest share of research and development in europe. on average, companies spend 4% on research and development, whereas the average european company spends only 2%. the commission has already made a number of proposals. the crisis has hit this industry hard in all sectors at the same time. this is the first time this has happened, we have never had this before, and i have to point out to you that the public is only concerned with the situation with passenger cars. the situation is much more dramatic in the commercial vehicle sector, where orders for the entire european union have been reduced to practically zero, with a production capacity of almost 40 000 commercial vehicles per month. the negative effects on employment will not be excluded, and this is mainly due to two factors. we have a clear overcapacity of motor vehicles in the european union. the industry itself admits that it is 20%. there are people who say it's much more than that. but 20% is a very high figure, and if you compare that to the number of people employed, we are talking about 400 000 jobs. there is no doubt that the structural measures long planned by european car manufacturers will be accelerated in the year of the crisis. i say this in all clarity and distinctness. there is no guarantee that we will have all the production sites in europe that we have today by the end of this year. the probability is high that we will not have a whole series of production sites at the end of this year. there is not even a guarantee that all european producers will be on the market by the end of this year. the international competitive pressure in the automobile industry is very strong. we have strengthened it here as european legislators by demanding that the european automobile industry performs significantly in the years to come. they must be able to innovate significantly. i would like to say, in order to avoid mrs harms criticising me again, that i am not criticising this, mrs harms, i think it is the right thing to do. don't accuse me of stating facts. i'm not criticizing, i'm just stating the obvious. we have made the european car considerably more expensive by our legislation, and it will become much more expensive in the coming years. the effect of this is to increase competitive pressure, to increase cost pressure and to increase the need for firms to increase productivity. it is the only way to survive in this competitive environment. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the situation in the automobile sector. it does not in any case lead to a positive employment effect. that's the situation we have. our policy now has two objectives. firstly, to get european industry through this crisis and - i emphasize every word - to avoid losing a single european manufacturer in the process. not one. the second is to strengthen the competitiveness of the european automotive industry in the long term and to establish europe as the leading automotive region in the world. as far as the measures in part i are concerned, we have done what could be done. we have opened up access to finance for the european automobile industry, which is particularly hard hit by the credit crunch. the european investment bank is providing nine billion euros for this industry alone this year, and i have to tell you, it makes no sense to ask for more here. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. nine billion are available. we have made the control of aid so flexible, thanks to the work of my colleague neelie kroes, and we have changed the rules so that member states have much more scope to react quickly and specifically when individual aid is needed. the commission is taking on the role that the law has given it, which is to ensure that these measures do not distort competition and do not jeopardise our policy objectives. i'll give you just one example. it is perfectly clear that aid to the european subsidiaries of american companies can only be approved if it is clear that it is intended solely to preserve jobs in europe. we have taken a number of measures to promote fleet renewal, while at the same time pursuing the objective of achieving a positive environmental effect. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the system of paying scrappage premiums is not applied by all member states, but those which do follow the principles we have already agreed on, namely that these measures must not be discriminatory against other producers. to give you another example: a member state cannot say: i will give you a premium if you scrap your old car, but the new car must be a german car if you live in germany, or a french car or a czech car. that's not possible. but it is possible, for example - and i would welcome this - to link such scrappage premiums to environmental objectives. to say that it will only be paid if the new car purchased is a car that meets certain emission standards. as far as we can see, this premium is working and therefore has the desired positive effect. there is only one way to get the commercial vehicle market moving. there are no scrappage premiums here, as you can imagine. the aim here is to provide access to finance, mainly for small and medium-sized enterprises in this sector. we are. and it is about ensuring that public investment gives priority to the procurement of environmentally friendly commercial vehicles, for example in public transport or other public services for which vehicles are needed. we've already done all that. in the long term - we have already discussed this in this house on several occasions - the recommendations in the cars 21 process are to ensure the future of the european automobile industry by making greater efforts in innovation, research and development, so that the european car of the future is the world's leading car not only in terms of technical standards, production standards and safety standards, but also in terms of fuel efficiency, i.e. consumption poverty, and environmental friendliness, i.e. low emissions. the european industry is also moving in this direction and we are supporting these projects under the european economic recovery programme, as you all know. in conclusion, let me say that the most important result of the consultation with the member states was that we gave each other a firm promise not to allow a protectionist race in europe. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. what we can still do to stimulate consumption and to guide the automobile industry through this crisis and help it through this crisis is to ensure that international conditions of competition are not also violated. this is a question that should be addressed to the united states in particular. we shall see what measures president obama takes to deal with the crisis in the american automobile industry. i would like to say this: we have no interest from a european point of view in the bankruptcy of the american car manufacturers. the consequences for europe would be devastating if that were to happen. we are not interested in an american policy which favours the american car industry at the difficult situation, but we firmly believe that it is capable and strong enough to cope with this difficult situation and to make an important contribution to creating and safeguarding jobs and the rapporteur. - mr president, i apologise to my colleagues and thank them for their patience. we should remember that for many years the european parliament has wanted to express its views on small and mediumsized enterprises, which account for 99% of all european enterprises and 75 million jobs, whereas today these small and mediumsized enterprises have access to the external market, outside the union, at 3% and 8% within the union. we therefore call on the council and the commission to deal with this reality in multilateral and bilateral negotiations, in access to foreign markets, in the fight against counterfeiting, in the use of trade defence instruments and in tendering procedures. trade brings them greater prosperity. i would like to thank my colleagues on the inta committee and especially the shadow rapporteurs of the two main groups, mr saïfi and mr locatelli, and also the secretariat and in particular dr bendini. i believe that with the work of all of us we are offering today to the european commission shared reflections and proposals on a subject which we know is dear to commissioner ashton, as he recalled in his investiture hearing, and which we must tackle immediately if we are to solve, at least in part, the great economic and financial crisis which is gripping our workers and citizens.
in writing. i am in favour of the report by mr dumitriu on information and promotion measures for agricultural products on the internal market and in third countries. i believe, as the commission has repeatedly said, that administrative procedures must be simplified within the european institutional framework. this regulation allows the community to carry out information measures on the internal market and on the markets of third countries for a number of agricultural products, while maintaining the specific characteristics of the measures depending on the place of implementation. i agree with the political decision that has been taken, which respects the needs of the member states, who are keen to promote an image of their agricultural products to consumers within the community and in third countries that is based primarily on quality, nutritional characteristics, food safety and production methods.
in writing. - i am voting against the report by mrs roure on the implementation in the eu of directive 2003/9/ec on the reception conditions for asylum seekers and refugees. in fact, although i regret that some visits have shown that the existing directives were still being poorly applied or were not being applied by some member states, i do not agree with the rapporteur when she says that there are various shortcomings in the level of reception conditions. i also disagree with the fact that the capacity of the first reception centres opened by some member states is poor and does not seem to meet the needs of migrants. finally, i do not agree with the request that asylum seekers be accommodated as a priority in open reception centres rather than in closed units.
in writing. - i support the report by mrs muscardini on the strengthening of the role of european smes in international trade. for the european union, which is dominated by small and mediumsized enterprises, the international presence of smes is crucial. at present, only 8% of smes have an international dimension and most exports remain within the european union. the few smes exporting outside the european union also tend to concentrate on mature and tending to be saturated markets such as the united states, canada and switzerland, while the presence of smes in emerging countries is low. the commission's proposal for a directive on the harmonization of the laws of the member states relating to the protection of employees in the event of the insolvency of their employer is a very good one.
in writing. - i give my vote in favour of the report by mr papastamkos on international trade and the internet. i agree with the rapporteur's aim of highlighting the areas of international trade in which the internet has acted as a catalyst, creating new conditions for the development of world trade. this is evident, because international trade and the internet influence each other in a very obvious way. i am also firmly convinced that the development of e-commerce is of considerable benefit to consumers. the main advantages, both at national and european level and worldwide, are the very wide choice of goods and services, competitive prices, a lower cost of living and a better quality of life. consumers are now able to compare products and services better, thanks to the availability of more information. access is available 24 hours a day from home or work.
in writing. - i shall vote in favour of the report by mr friedrich-wilhelm graefe zu baringdorf on the placing on the market and use of feedingstuffs. i agree with the proposal, which provides for a radical overhaul of european legislation on animal feed, involving not only the simplification of existing rules but also the adaptation of that legislation to the provisions applicable to food. among the main aspects, i am absolutely in favour of the indication of the raw materials present in compound feedingstuffs and their exact quantity (the so-called 'open declaration'), which was one of the main requests made by the european parliament following the bovine spongiform encephalopathy (bse) crisis. finally, i agree with the rapporteur on the protection of the consumer's right to information and the labelling of such feedingstuffs.
in writing. - i am voting in favour of the report by mr schröder on the impact of economic partnership agreements (epas) on development. the launch agreements signed so far are only the beginning of a long and fruitful cooperation with these non-european countries. in the case of the epas, a 15-year liberalisation process was considered acceptable by both the eu and the acp countries. in addition, the minimum requirement for virtually all areas of trade to be liberalised should not be less than 80% of trade between the partners. finally, i am convinced that the development of further agreements will only improve the economic situation of both parties.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased and proud that the european parliament is examining the subject of the social market economy and is deciding on concrete proposals to give effective support to this sector. the purpose of my report is threefold. the first: the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the creation of a european network of national experts. 10% of european enterprises belong to this sector and also 9 and 10% of employment. it is a reality made up of different actors - cooperatives, mutual funds, foundations, social enterprises, associations - that share specific values and contribute significantly to gdp. so, to give a clearer and more transparent institutional visibility. second purpose: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. a different way of doing business, producing, consuming and employing people, a different but fully fledged way of doing business in the market. it is a way of life characterized by certain distinctive features which must not be reduced to the bare minimum and which essentially consist in the desire to associate and reconcile production and work with the values of solidarity, responsibility and the dignity of the person, also in the world of work. some people say, and i think this is very effective, that these companies operate with capital but not for capital. these are concepts which are part of the ideal of the european union based on the delors' thinking because we have often recognized the social economy as the keystone of the european social model, but little has been done in practice. today is also the most appropriate time to rediscover the relevance of these enterprises, because the current crisis in production has revealed that many traditional economic actors are very fragile, very weak and sometimes very unfavourable. this world of the social economy is more closely linked to the territory, the real economy and the individual, and is therefore protected, as it has always been, from the temptation to speculate. it's also an industry that has very different subjects, which have a lot to do with welfare as well. it's also called the social world, the pole of social utility, and it can help, i think, the sustainability of our social systems in times of constraint. third purpose: i would like to ask the commissioner what he thinks of the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks of exposure to carcinogens. i am only making a few suggestions very briefly. first, definitions must be clarified to understand accurately the profiles and definitions of these very different subjects. it is also needs a definition of its own. the commission has done something in this respect with a manual, but it is absolutely necessary to implement it. and in this direction i think that the world of academia, research, universities can contribute. finally, what legislative initiatives, if any, are needed. several things have been done - the statutes of the cooperative, the statutes of the foundation - and i have seen that the commission has resumed consultation. so, you have to figure out what it takes and whether you need to continue down this path. we do not want to see the bureaucratization of an industry that lives on idealism, motivation and freedom. but where community rules are needed, or were needed, it would be good to have them. finally, a call for involvement in madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased that the rapporteur, mr van den burg, and the whole of parliament will support this proposal to amend the provisions of the vat directive. finally, a proposal which will guarantee equal opportunities for all member states and improve the functioning of the internal market with regard to reduced vat rates and which also intelligently respects subsidiarity, since it leaves the states the possibility of applying reduced vat rates to labour-intensive and locally provided services, such as those of greatest social significance relating to housing, personal assistance, etc., and more generally applicable to the benefit of small and mediumsized enterprises. i therefore share the rapporteur's hope that this instrument will provide a tax system that promotes employment, increases productivity and reduces the underground economy.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, when the european parliament set up vat, it has always followed its evolution, both in terms of its harmonization between the member states, its adjustment to cope with economic circumstances and the transitional derogations granted to the countries which have recently joined the european union. the approach, although global, has thus been characterized by the necessary flexibility in the application of the rates in question, to take account both of the specific nature of the productive sectors and of economic and social considerations. the proposal under consideration, however, is designed to extend the scope of reduced vat rates to a number of services, such as labour-intensive services, catering, local services, housing construction and sales, and services for disadvantaged groups. far from the objective of harmonizing vat in all the member states, the directive in question, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, seeks to ensure equal opportunities for all the member states, while at the same time giving them autonomy in fixing reduced rates. it follows that consumers would thus be induced to transfer some activities carried out in the context of the local or underground economy to the official economy, thus promoting economic growth without distorting the functioning of the internal market. it should be remembered, however, that for most of the services in question, a reduced rate is already available, albeit only in a limited number of member states and for a limited period of time. however, the debate on the application of reduced rates for the protection of the environment and energy saving is still open, and the commission will have to provide specific assessments on this subject, given the importance of these sectors in the european union's economy.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the proposal to extend the scope of reduced vat to certain labour-intensive services, such as catering, maintenance and construction, represents an important opportunity for positive economic effects on the market and on employment, especially in a period of such serious economic crisis, such as the one we are experiencing. there will be no change in competition, but the opportunity will be to give a small boost to production and stimulate consumption, to create new jobs and to help businesses and households. in my view, further extensions of the scope of the reduced vat, for example to include so-called 'green services', would be desirable, precisely to promote environmental policies. but as far as the text we are going to vote on is concerned, the proposal to reduce vat on diapers and childcare services is particularly welcome. this parliament has on several occasions called on the commission and the member states to coordinate macroeconomic and social policies more closely, precisely in order to respond to the increase in new poverty. we cannot help remembering that at the moment about 17% of european families live below the poverty line and one in five children is poor. the council has now the floor, and i hope it will approve this proposal as soon as possible and open a wider and more ambitious debate to promote tax policies that are tailored to the needs of businesses, but also to the needs of families, and perhaps to extend the vat reduction to all children's products.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think we must solve this small business crisis in a genuinely european way. we are seeing a dying of small and medium-sized enterprises across the continent and this dying is due to lack of access to credit. the problem is that banks do not give any credit to business and it is also true that attempts by some governments to finance banks so that they, in turn, finance small businesses, are proving to be a failure because no one knows what debts are actually hitting banks at this moment. i therefore propose that the national states, by nationalising their national banks, should promote the printing of money, or of vouchers corresponding to money, to finance small businesses. this type of attempt has been made recently by the republic of taiwan, which issued vouchers, which are practically equivalent to money, and gave them, in the form of vouchers to individuals, to citizens, in the republic of taiwan. this has basically allowed the issuance of 3 billion dollars or euros in the republic of taiwan. we have to do the same thing: we must give credit to small businesses by issuing money as states, not on debt but on credit.
