the agenda includes statements by the council and the commission on the new visa rules for the countries of the western balkans (the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, montenegro and serbia).
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, some areas of the balkans are still today unstable and illegal trafficking routes are under the control of organized crime. trafficking in human beings is particularly serious, often involving exploitation through black labour or prostitution. visa liberalisation must therefore be accompanied by strict application of security rules, one of which is the introduction of biometric passports. albania and bosnia-herzegovina have apparently not yet fully implemented these technical measures. it is therefore essential that visa liberalisation does not take place in respect of these two countries until there is full cooperation by the governments and the implementation of technical measures to ensure the identity of the persons concerned. in my opinion, lack of qualifications does not constitute discrimination.

author of the book. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the dairy sector is going through one of the most serious and profound phases of the last decades: the fall in milk prices and the more general emergency in the milk market have now become a source of concern throughout europe; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the milk market is not affected by the crisis. milk prices have fallen everywhere, reaching an average of 24 cents a litre in the european union. the situation of many economic operators is even more dire, with prices below 21-20 cents against economic costs of no less than 40 cents per litre. alarming signs are also emerging in other markets, such as cereals, olive oil and fruit and vegetables. on this front, first of all, we must continue to make use of all the measures at our disposal to stabilize the market and stimulate consumption, but at the same time we must be able to look to the future with medium- and on behalf of the efd group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to express my doubts about the proposal to extend the 2009-2010 intervention period for butter and skimmed milk powder, as this proposal risks turning short-term measures, which are necessary in the context of the current market crisis, into structural measures which would in fact return the milk market to the pre-quota situation. in order to give a better balance to market measures, not only benefiting the member states concerned by the production of butter and skimmed milk powder, i call for the reintroduction of community aid for the private storage of long-aged cheeses. finally, i would like to draw your attention to the issue of indication of origin and labelling of dairy products and the traceability of products: this is a demand that is coming directly from european consumers in an increasing way and that would help us to deal with the crisis in the dairy sector. i hope that the other groups will support this proposal.
member of the commission. − mr president, first of all i would like to thank members of parliament for this very dedicated debate. i have actually listened very carefully. but of course i have also noted the different views that i have heard among the different members of this parliament. as regards the quota system; it seems to be the scapegoat of this whole situation in which we find ourselves. i do not underestimate – and i have been very precise on this since the very beginning of the discussion – that the dairy sector, not only in europe but globally, finds itself in an unprecedented crisis. that must be very clear. so i certainly do understand the frustration that i see among farmers in different parts of europe, not all over, but in different parts of europe. the abolition of the quota system was decided back in 2003 so it is not a decision that was taken overnight while nobody knew what was happening. then, in the health check, we had the discussion on increasing the quotas to try to find a soft landing for the dairy farmers. but i think that those who want to point their finger at the quota system for being the reason for all the problems in which dairy farmers find themselves are wrong. because we see that even with a quota system in place, we have not been able to maintain high prices and the structural changes in the dairy sector have taken place anyway. if you look at 1984, when the quota system was introduced, we had 1.6 million dairy farmers in the old eu-10. today in eu-10 we have 300 000 dairy farmers: less than one fifth of the number of dairy farmers today compared to 1984 with a quota system in place. so these structural changes are taking place anyway. i do not think that going back or rolling back the decision in the health check is the right policy, and here i am supported by all heads of state saying clearly in their decisions from the meeting in june that i have to stick to the decisions from the health check. i have never, ever, during the health check discussions, signalled any openness to roll back these decisions because that would certainly jeopardise predictability for farmers within the european union. but, josé bové, i think you said i had not been acting with preciseness; that is, the laissez-faire attitude. i do not think it is fair to say that we have been doing nothing. i am not going to repeat all the different measures that we have been taking. i think that, if member states want to pay specific attention to the dairy sector, they now have the possibility with the health check to reallocate the direct payments so they give a special preference to the grassland areas. that is a possibility and i know that at least one big member state has taken the opportunity to use this possibility, and for the mountainous areas there are lots of different possibilities. we have production in europe today that is 45% below quota, so what would happen if we actually wanted to cut quota by 5%? we would actually damage the situation for the young farmers that have invested in the future. therefore, i would recommend to those countries, those member states, who really want to help their dairy sector that they use this buy-up of quotas from those who want to leave the dairy sector. that is a much better way of securing the maintenance of those who have invested while giving a helping hand to those that want to leave the sector. that is i think the right policy. could i then just correct the misunderstanding on the super levy? we are not introducing a new super levy system. we are just giving the possibility that, if member states are buying up quotas from farmers, they can reduce the number of kilos or tonnes from their ceiling, but it is not a new super levy that will punish any of the farmers. just on some of the promotion. we have already reserved eur 14 million for promotion for the rest of this year. we have agreed on extending the school milk scheme; yogurt that is low in sugar – that is, containing no more than 7% sugar – will now be introduced into the school milk scheme. labelling – i hear from different members of parliament that there is interest in a labelling system. let us discuss that in the context of the quality paper that is actually on the table at the moment. so i think there are lots of possibilities. then, finally, on the food chain, i completely agree with you that that there is no transparency in this chain and we cannot see where the added value is disappearing. therefore, i am looking forward to the presenting of this report before the end of the year so we can see what the situation actually looks like. i must say that, if you look at the supermarket situation all over europe, there are huge differences. germany has a tradition or number of discount supermarkets. these supermarkets are using dairy or milk products, drinking milk as a produit d'appel to get the consumers in, and they are offering a very low price but they are just handing over the bill to the farmers, paying them the low price. so, i think it would be very interesting and necessary to see what is actually happening in this chain, so let us get this transparency on the table and let us, internally in the commission, but also in member states’ competition authorities, look into the market. it has been a very interesting discussion here today. i hope that you have noticed the short-term measures and the long-term measures that have been worked out together with france and germany. i am sure that we will have some very interesting discussions on the future of the dairy sector in europe because we all want our dairy sector to have a future.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i agree with commissioner piebalgs. its recent statements confirm that southstream is not a competitor to nabucco but a further contribution to the diversification of europe's energy supply sources. european energy security is based on a variety of sources, routes and countries of supply. future demand is estimated to grow by 100 to 150 billion m3 of additional gas from now to 2020. in view of these considerations, the development of various options is a necessity and southstream is not an alternative to nabucco but an addition. the commission considers the southern corridor as a set of projects including nabucco, southstream and the turkey, greece, italy (itg) interconnection. the anti-russian polemic is therefore in contradiction with what we shall see in the coming years. it is important that the european parliament should call for pragmatism and above all for consistency in the choices that the european union has already made: the european economic recovery plan, decision 1364/2006 of the european parliament and of the council of 13 december 2006 laying down guidelines for trans-european networks in the field of energy and the second energy security strategy. the diversification of sources, routes and countries of supply is the real pillar of europe's energy security policy and the southstream-nabucco challenge, beyond the political and economic interests of the various countries most directly involved, must be analysed realistically, without the distorting lenses of ideology but rather with a clear vision of what needs to be done.

member of the commission. − mr president, freedom of expression and freedom of information represent a foundation of a free, democratic and pluralistic society. that is my firm believe as a former journalist and it is also the firm belief of the european union. that is why all the eu institutions – parliament, the council and the commission – have signed up to the eu charter of fundamental rights, article 11 of which states that: ‘everyone has the right to freedom of expression. this right shall include freedom to hold opinions and to receive and impart information and ideas without interference by public authority and regardless of frontiers. the freedom and pluralism of the media shall be respected.’ i would like to recall that the eu charter also states, in article 51(1), where and when those fundamental rights apply. i quote again: ‘the provisions of this charter are addressed to the institutions, bodies, offices and agencies of the union with due regard for the principle of subsidiarity and to the member states’, but ‘only when they are implementing union law’. within the eu’s sphere of competence, which we have to respect, the european commission has always stood up for freedom of the media, freedom of expression, freedom of information and freedom of the press, whether within the eu or in our external relations with third countries. i recall in particular the important role played by the eu’s ‘television without frontiers’ directive, which since 1989 has made sure that citizens in all eu member states are free to receive, without restrictions, broadcasts from other eu countries; an eu directive which has substantially contributed to the free flow of information across borders and to a more pluralistic media landscape in all member states. in this context i would like to thank the european parliament for having helped the commission to get a modernised version of this directive which extends the freedom of information across borders, beyond broadcasting, to other audiovisual services and particularly those transmitted by internet. this directive needs to be implemented by all eu member states by the end of the year, and will make important contributions to a pluralistic landscape when it also comes to the online environment. let me also recall three other very important elements of this directive. firstly, the promotion of independent tv productions. there is a rule in the directive that broadcasters need to reserve at least 10% of their transmission time or 10% of their programming budget to european works created by producers who are independent from the broadcasters. secondly, the directive foresees in its modernised version the right of journalists and news organisations to access short extracts across the eu for the purpose of short reporting. thirdly, and this is of utmost importance, there is a reference in the new directive to the need to have independent media authorities at national level. this is a reference which was proposed by the commission and which could only be adopted in the end thanks to strong support by the european parliament. thus, for the broadcasting sector, the modernised television without frontiers directive can be seen as a charter for freedom of cross-border information in the eu. now let me recall another important aspect in the eu’s field of competence where this institution can act and has acted for the benefit of media pluralism. i mean radio spectrum policy. you all know that there cannot be broadcasting without access to radio spectrum, and it is the eu policy to ensure that all players on the market get non-discriminatory access to radio spectrum. national authorities are thus not entitled to freeze, by means of spectrum allocation, the competitive situation on the media market for the benefit of the operators already active on that market. the european court of justice, by the way, has confirmed this important principle, which directly results from the freedom to provide services, in its centro europa judgment. the commission welcomed that ruling as a contribution to fair competition and as an important foundation for strengthening media pluralism. on that basis, the commission has repeatedly acted against member states where the system of spectrum management has appeared to be in contradiction with this principle. by way of example, i would like to recall the 2006 infringement proceedings on radio spectrum allocation in italy, which my colleague neelie kroes and i opened. under the pressure of this procedure, the italian authorities are now changing their approach. the result of this will be a substantial market opening and a win for media pluralism. spectrum policy is therefore a clear example of an area where the eu can act within its field of competences in order to enhance competition for the resources on which broadcasters depend, and thereby strengthen media pluralism. concerning the written press, the competences of the eu are substantially more limited. the written press is one of those prime examples of national, or even regional, competences and its situation very often reflects the varying cultural traditions in our different member states. there is thus no eu legislation specifically on the written press, nor can there be legislation under the treaties as they stand. nevertheless, in the eu institutions, and in particular the european commission, we have always flanked the development of the written press across the eu. i recall that in my capacity as eu media commissioner i had numerous meetings with editors-in-chief from all around europe to discuss the current issues relating to media freedom and media pluralism. in june 2009, this led to the european charter on freedom of the press, drafted by the journalists across europe. i fully endorsed that charter when the final outcome of this work was handed over to me. the charter on the freedom of the press initiated by the european journalist community is an important reaffirmation of the basic values enshrined in fundamental legal texts such as the eu charter of fundamental rights. it is also a reminder for all policymakers in their field of competence that, in order to have effective freedom of the press, public authorities do indeed have a role to play: they must be ready to protect freedom of expression and foster its development. the charter is therefore an important step towards reinforcing these basic values and rights, allowing journalists to invoke them against governments or against political public authorities whenever they feel that the freedom of their work is unjustifiably threatened. the honourable members will see that strong political commitment is being shown by the eu’s institutions, and particularly by the commission, to fundamental rights and freedom of information, of expression and of the media. we are using our competences to uphold those rights and freedoms in our work, on the basis of the treaties, and will continue to do so. however, let me also touch on another important aspect, namely the fact that fundamental rights apply to eu policies does not make the eu competent for all matters relating to fundamental rights in one member state or another. let us not forget that the member states have constitutions, many of them with long traditions, and that in all member states there are courts, appeal courts and constitutional courts which ensure that fundamental rights are respected and enforced whenever national authorities act. we had an example of this as recently as yesterday in italy. this is the result of the fact that we have a division of labour, because europe is not a superstate, but is comprised of 27 sovereign member states and will continue to operate like this under the new lisbon treaty too. i would therefore call on you not to make use of the eu institutions to solve problems which should, under our treaties, be solved at national level. we should not claim a role that we do not have, and we will not have it under the lisbon treaty either. let us concentrate here on applying effectively the rules, principles, rights and freedoms in areas where the eu is competent. this can lead to very important progress, and i have mentioned several concrete examples of this in my speech. let me add another example of where we could act. paul rübig, a member of this house, recently proposed in a budgetary amendment a new eu programme called erasmus for journalists. such a programme would, in difficult times for the written press, allow journalists to work for a limited time with editorial staff in other member states. it would also allow journalists to discover the political, economic and social situation in other member states and to write about it. it would allow journalists to compare the situation across europe and to present that to the readers, including the situation with regard to freedom of the press. that is why i encourage the european parliament to look very favourably on these proposals, which certainly have the support of the eu media commissioner.
i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in the negotiations, but that it should be involved in the negotiations. "remember that you have a great responsibility, that we have a great responsibility", to make your country better. we know that our countries will be better off if europe is stronger, able to respond with a sense of justice to the expectations of its citizens. we know that this is possible if we all do it together, of course; i am not saying that we should not be concerned about the future of the community, but that we should be concerned about the future of the community. so many controversies affect my country but i want to reassure everyone right away that we are talking about a great democratic country, which has a great constitution. yesterday was a very important day for us italians, because the constitutional court, in the face of outrages and demands for impunity, reaffirmed a simple and ancient principle, namely that all citizens are equal before the law. but we know that even large countries can be distracted, can confuse public goods with private interests. but we cannot afford to let the nation states weaken. the right to free information, without pressure or conditioning by government authorities, must be guaranteed and this is a public good, a good for everyone, in every country. and this good must be defended without hesitation by the union. we must work to provide common standards, to set limits beyond which information is no longer considered free. it is urgent that the union should take action, that a directive be adopted to define indicators on pluralism and the defence of a good which must be available to all. mrs reding, you must never forget that we are a parliament and not a museum where you store moldy objects.

(the president again requested silence)in my introductory speech i also underlined the very clear actions, the concrete examples of where the eu can act and has acted, and i underlined the problems which have to be solved at national level. the constitutional court of italy, which acted yesterday, has clearly shown what that means. now there have been several clear demands by this house and i would like to reply to these if the house would permit and listen. (the president once more requested silence)there is the demand by this house to go for the media pluralism approach which has been promised. the work on media pluralism has already made substantial progress and we have published the second step with the risk indicators on media pluralism. maybe many parliamentarians have not seen these. they are on the internet; they can be looked at and they are a very important element in being able to conduct this objective work on media pluralism that the parliament has called for. i must say that i was very disappointed because we had a public workshop on this and not a single parliamentarian turned up to participate in the workshop. well, the risk indicators have been published now and they can be looked at. they will be the basis for our future work. second question: why does not the commission activate article 7 of the eu treaty in the case of italy? first of all, article 7 is a very exceptional provision. so far it has never been activated by the eu institutions. this clause would apply only if there were a complete breakdown of national jurisdictional orders and fundamental rights systems in a given member state. i do not think that we have reached such a situation in any of our member states. but – and it is very interesting – the article states that the european parliament itself has the possibility to activate article 7 of the eu treaty. so i call on the european parliament, if it really thinks there is sufficient proof, to activate article 7 of the eu treaty. third question: many parliamentarians from all political parties – and i think there is relative unanimity in this house – have asked for an eu directive on media pluralism and media concentration. (the president once more requested silence) this is a fundamental question that has to be discussed in depth. you might recall that the european commission started to work on the draft for such a directive in the 1990s and you will also recall that all member states without exception were against such a directive at that time because it was considered to be outside the competences of the eu. now, maybe the situation has changed today and there will be a large majority of member states thinking this can enter into the competences of the eu. of course it would be possible to arrive at such a very generous interpretation of the treaty, to allow the eu to tackle the matter. but, before even starting to think about this, the commission would need to have the strong support of the whole european parliament. and i would like the european parliament to identify clearly which internal market problems it wants to be tackled with such a directive. you know that i personally am not the kind of commissioner who has a problem in regulating. i have in the last five years regulated when it was necessary. but to do this we need clear evidence about the questions we want to answer. would legislation solve the problems you all have in mind today? could we justify it under existing eu competences? is there a clear cross-border dimension? is there a clear internal market dimension because – remember – the legislation which we have already put on the table was all on the internal market legal basis. all this would need to be clarified before we could start a legislative process. so i invite the parliament to discuss this seriously and i invite the parliament to respond to this question in an own-initiative report adopted by a majority of members. then the commission will take that a step forward. in the meantime the commission has done its homework by establishing the risk indicators that will help us to analyse this whole problem in all member states on an objective basis. i think, in the end, that is what the parliament wants. that is also what the other institution wants, because we do not want political usage of our basic freedoms. we want these freedoms to be a right; we want these freedoms to be a basic value and to be treated as such. in writing. to declare that freedom of information is denied in italy is an offense, instrumental and opportunistic, to one of the largest western democracies. freedom of information is denied in those countries where dictatorial regimes prevent their subjects from increasing their awareness of daily events by choosing the source of information considered to be the most authoritative. the internet has the merit of breaking down all political, geographical, economic and social barriers to access to information in countries with a democratic tradition such as italy. in some countries, by contrast, the internet is filtered, and many sites, considered non-governmental, are blocked. there, civil rights, such as freedom of expression, marriage, assembly, rights of which we in the west perhaps no longer even realize the importance, because we are used to them, do not even come close to the concept of inalienability guaranteed by our constitution. because they simply don't exist. the european parliament must be a place for growth, debate and the exchange of good practice between european countries. it cannot be reduced to a privileged theatre setting where you can stage a free "premiere" of any provincial play. if there is to be a debate on freedom of the press in europe, it must take place in the european parliament, and let there be one, but let it be constructive and worthy of the prestige of the institution of which we are honoured to be a part.
in writing. - i would like to congratulate parliament for having prevented, at my request, the postponement yesterday of the vote on the mobilisation of the solidarity fund in support of the earthquake in abruzzo last april, which caused very serious damage to people and property. there was really no reason to postpone, even for two weeks, a vote which has such a major impact on the lives of european citizens in difficulty. the european commission had carried out the investigation in a very short time, granting italy the exact amount requested, namely eur 493 771 159, which could be the highest amount ever granted by this fund. with this vote, parliament therefore shows its full solidarity and closeness to the people affected. the average time for disbursing this fund is normally about 18 months. the consultation of parliament has now been completed in a very short time, considering that the earthquake occurred only five months ago. i therefore strongly hope that the commission and the council will reduce the remaining time in the procedure as much as possible and make the funds available to italy before the end of the year.

change course. so far, it can be assumed that the vis system has a good architecture and that there are indeed some bugs, but these can be corrected. however, it is these tests which will then determine whether the contract needs to be terminated at the contractor's expense. it is too early to say, and the calendar would then be revised at that time. i would remind you that in 2005 the first region on the date set by the commission when all member states have notified the commission that they have made the necessary technical and legal arrangements to use the vis in that region. this implies that the vis starts operations in the first region - north africa, which covers countries with the highest risks in terms of irregular immigration or security - on the same date for all member states. this leads me to say that it is really necessary that all the member states should be able to operate the vis, because it would be extremely damaging if the central system were to acting president of the council. - mr president, commissioner, elmar brok, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. the development of the european external action service is a matter which i know is of great interest to you here in parliament. i have read with great interest and enthusiasm the report by mr elmar brok, which was approved by the committee on constitutional affairs on monday. of course, we on the presidency side fully agree with what elmar brok writes, that the foreign service is indeed the key to our joint work to make european foreign policy an active and more cohesive body so that european policy can be seen in a better way around the world. the idea is to bridge the gap that has existed between the work of the commission and that of the council, so that the union's policies are oriented in the same direction. this is necessary for us to be as efficient as possible. that's why it's important that we give the foreign service the best possible start. this is one of the greatest and most important challenges of the lisbon treaty. there are many pieces of the puzzle to be put in place, and therefore extensive preparatory work is under way in the council. the aim is to enable the european council to agree on a report which the high representative, once appointed, will be able to base on when presenting his proposal on the eeas. in this work, the european parliament will of course be consulted when the high representative presents his proposal. in the meantime, the presidency will ensure that there is a regular dialogue with the european parliament. we have had such a dialogue so far and we will continue to have it. it is important that the european parliament, the council and the commission have regular contact on these issues, not only at the level of officials but also at the political level. immediately after the irish referendum - we are very pleased that the result was a 'yes' - the member states and the commission began a very intensive work to prepare the european external action service. this work is progressing and i am fully confident that we will be able to put forward a number of useful ideas for the future high representative to the european council next week. since it is the high representative's task to present the final proposal, he or she will of course be involved in the work as soon as he or she has been appointed. this is very important so that he or she can also shape the proposal. the presidency will present an agreement of principle covering five major elements. the scope of the eeas's activities, its legal status, staffing, financing and the eu delegations are all covered. we are not yet finished, the discussions are still ongoing, but i would like to share with you some thoughts on how far we have come at the moment, and here there seems to be a great deal of agreement between the council and the commission, and i hope eventually also with the european parliament. as regards the scope of the eeas, it is clear that geographical and thematic 'desk functions' should be established, which have collective responsibility for tasks currently handled by the commission and the council secretariat. the commission will continue to have primary responsibility for trade, aid and enlargement issues, although the exact line of demarcation between the commission and the eeas on aid issues remains to be defined. the member states and the commission further agree that the legal status of the eeas should reflect and support the unique role, sui generis, of the eeas in the eu system. whatever the legal solution that is ultimately reached, it must respect the principles of good administration and accountability. staff will be recruited from the commission, the council secretariat and the member states. this is clearly stated in the treaty of lisbon. all these three categories of staff shall be entitled to take up their duties on equivalent terms. the eu delegations will be placed under the chairmanship of the high representative as soon as the treaty of lisbon enters into force. an important issue in the establishment of the european external action service is the liaison with the european parliament. once in place, the high representative will regularly consult the european parliament on the broad lines and key policy choices of the common foreign and security policy, as well as the common security and defence policy. i am sure that close contacts with the european parliament will also be developed at the level of officials. the european external action service should therefore have a function responsible for liaising with parliament. this is about as far as we've gotten in the discussions. i cannot go into more detail because we are not yet finished with the talks, but we will do everything to keep the european parliament informed of the progress being made. the high representative has not been appointed yet, so the thoughts are just thoughts, nothing more. in the end, it is he or she who will put forward the proposal in accordance with the provisions of the treaty. i would like to thank you for the opportunity to speak and look forward to a fruitful debate in which i will of course listen very carefully to parliament's views and answer questions to the best of my ability.
member of the commission. − mr president, we are, i hope, on the very last lap of the process of bringing the treaty of lisbon into force, completing a process which has taken eight years of discussions and negotiations. after the decisive result of the irish referendum, we all hope that the czech ratification can finally follow very soon. if we achieve this on the 20th anniversary of the reunification of europe, it will be a great day for europe and its citizens – not least because we will be able to focus all our attention on the pressing challenges and policy concerns that lie ahead of us. as we reach the final stages, allow me to congratulate parliament, and particularly the constitutional affairs committee, with elmar brok as rapporteur, on delivering its opinion on the key element of the lisbon treaty which is the external european action service. the creation of the eeas offers the european union and all its component institutions the chance to achieve what we have long hoped for: to have a common voice in the world and to strengthen the eu’s influence in the world. mr brok’s report recognises this great potential. together with this important debate and many other consultations with parliament representatives, it provides vital input to our work with the swedish presidency, but also with the member states and the council secretariat, over the coming months. i am happy to confirm that the commission strongly supports the parliament’s overall approach. i agree with the principles of transparency, democracy and coherence that you have just mentioned. it is obviously important that all the institutions work together to help the newly-appointed high representative vice-president in his or her task of preparing the decision on the creation of an eeas – a decision which, as you know, requires the consent of the commission and the consultation of the parliament. firstly, let me mention the status of the eeas. indeed it will be sui generis as there is no model to follow. we are building something new. it will neither be intergovernmental nor purely based on the community method, but we must ensure that the new system has a genuinely european approach inspired by and grounded in the strengths of community policies, as again was mentioned. the key question for us all is what the eeas should be able to deliver. this should be our objective. by bringing together the various actors in the field of external relations, we can ensure that our relations with the outside world are clear, coherent and driven by a single set of policy goals. it must carry authority as the core of eu external policy, the place where policy is developed and coordinated. it must also be seen to be such, both from inside and from outside the european union, and the eeas will only be effective if it works well with other institutions and fully respects the interinstitutional balance. this is why i think it is very important that the eeas should be set up in a way which allows it to work very closely with the commission and the council and to respect the need to be fully accountable to the european parliament. for the parliament, the bringing together of external action responsibilities into a single service will, i believe, mean a step change in parliament’s capacity to fulfil its role of scrutinising union policy. like the service itself, the way in which parliament relates to the service and to the high representative vice-president will also, in a way, have to be sui generis. the creation of the eeas will require a variety of decisions, probably including changes to the financial regulation and the staff regulations, both of which require a commission proposal and adoption through codecision.the high representative vice-president needs the authority to manage the service, but the service also needs to serve the eu system as a whole – most obviously the president of the european commission and the president of the european council, as well as the other commissioners with a role in external relations. it must be able to offer its assistance, both in brussels and in third countries, to the european parliament and to its official delegations which travel abroad. the close involvement of the member states in the new service is one of its key innovations. the coreper ambassadors are looking at how best to ensure that high-quality member states’ diplomats can be brought into the service early. we in the commission are examining how this may be done pending the modification of the staff regulations, and appointment to the service should be through selection procedures based on merit, with appropriate account being taken of the need for a geographic and gender balance. this very much meets the wishes expressed in the report. we also believe that all members of the eeas, whether officials of the eu institutions or member states’ officials on temporary contracts, should enjoy the same rights. they will be equal in every sense. as for the scope of the service, it needs to have a comprehensive overview of the union’s relations with the rest of the world, so it needs geographical desks as well as horizontal services to cover questions such as cfsp and csdp, human rights and relations with un bodies. the aim is to prevent duplication and to ensure that all those responsible for delivering eu external policy work effectively together, and the commission will also continue to have services responsible for trade, development policy, aid implementation, humanitarian aid and enlargement. it will also, of course, continue to drive the external aspects of the union’s key internal policies, and a central question in the current debate is how to manage the programming of external assistance. i can assure parliament that the eu’s development policy, including poverty eradication, will be a central part of the commission’s external activities. the high representative vice-president and the commissioner for development will work extremely closely together on this. the fact that the new high representative will also be a vice-president of the commission, responsible for coordinating all of the eu’s external action, will help. the service will also be responsible for the administration of delegations, though the people inside delegations will come, as now, from different services – not just the eeas, but also the commission services and maybe other institutions and bodies of the european union. from the entry into force of the treaty, commission delegations will become eu delegations. this will give them new responsibilities, but it will not diminish their role in representing the full range of commission activities. the eu delegations should be responsible for representation, coordination and negotiation as from the day the treaty comes into force. in most places, this procedure will go quite smoothly. however, in some, where the workload is particularly heavy, it will be necessary to organise a form of burden-sharing, not only with the rotating presidency but also with other member states. the creation of an entirely new external service is a major undertaking. it will, as your report says, evolve over time. we will learn together. our first aim must be that during the period between the entry into force of the treaty and the coming into being of the eeas, the effective delivery of the eu’s external policies is maintained. we and the council secretariat will work together with the high representative vice-president to ensure that there is no gap. but we need to look further. we will be bringing together officials and diplomats from the different institutions and all the member states. as we know, a common foreign policy is not just the sum of 27 national policies. we need people within the eeas who, while not losing their distinctive national ties, think european. we therefore need to create an eu diplomatic culture and an eu esprit de corps. for this, training is essential. the report raises the promising idea of the creation of a european diplomatic academy. in the mean time, we can make good use of the member states’ diplomatic academies. i very recently attended the 10th anniversary of the european diplomatic programme, which has anticipated and shown the way. it is worth remarking that since the 1970s the commission has already organised training seminars for more than 5 700 diplomats. one of the tasks of the eeas will be to establish a training strategy to ensure that all members, whatever their background, will be equipped to carry out their tasks. heads of delegations in particular will have to be able not only to carry out their political role, but also to handle all the commission activities that are such a substantial part of a delegation’s mandate. mr brok’s report also raises the question of whether consular services might be covered by the eeas. the commission is open to this idea even if it may take some time to develop. these are matters for the future. for the present, it is a challenge for us to ensure that the eeas functions well and in the interests of all: the european citizens, the member states and the european union. the commission supports the creation of the eeas, wants it to succeed, and will contribute in every way possible to ensure that it does so. this report shows that parliament will do the same. i am sorry to have been a little long, but i think this is such an important matter. please forgive me, mr president.

member of the commission. − mr president, i am happy to have the opportunity today to address you in plenary session on the proposal for a regulation on origin marking. this is a proposal which honourable members may recall the parliament has been a strong supporter of since its adoption by the college as long ago as december 2005. i particularly recall your resolution of july 2006 and the written declaration of september 2007. i was privileged to discuss this issue last month in strasbourg with a group of meps who stressed to me the need to move rapidly to adopt this regulation. i think honourable members would agree that it is of fundamental importance that trade policy not only strengthens the opportunities that open markets can offer but also addresses the concerns globalisation generates not just for consumers, but also, and perhaps particularly, for small enterprises. origin marking should therefore be considered in that spirit. in the 2007 declaration you emphasised the right of european consumers to have clear and immediate information about their purchases. that is precisely what this regulation is about. it aims to allow eu consumers to be fully aware of the country of origin of the products that they purchase. the commission has proposed a compulsory indication of the country of origin of certain products imported into the european union from third countries. not all products are covered – we focused on those of real interest, following a broad consultation with consumers and with industry. origin marking, i might add, is fully in line with the current wto rules and principles and something that exists almost everywhere in the world. imports into the united states, into canada, china and japan are subject to country-of-origin marking. as a matter of fact, most products that you can currently purchase in shops in the european union already bear the country-of-origin mark, as most legal systems currently require it. this means, of course, that for the vast majority of businesses an obligation to mark products exported to the european union will entail no additional cost. since 2006, discussions have been held in council in order to reach an agreement on the commission proposal. a number of member states remain to be convinced. they are worried that the administrative burden and the costs of an origin marking scheme may outweigh the benefits. we have taken due note of those concerns, and we have recently presented concrete options that we believe address those issues. this is not a new formal proposal; it is an attempt to find common ground and reach a compromise. a commission options paper was discussed with the member states in the article 133 committee on 23 october 2009. first of all, the commission asked the member states to consider the option of narrowing the product coverage – so as to include only end-consumer goods. the original list contained some intermediate products, such as raw skin and certain textiles, that are not of direct interest to the consumer. the commission suggests now to include only those goods that consumers can find in retail stores. secondly, the commission suggested that the scheme be launched on a pilot project basis. any continuation would be subject to an evaluation of the impact the proposed scheme had. this would allow for an assessment of the impact on cost and on price – it may also of course give some indication of how we could modify the product coverage of the regulation. i am pleased to say that the member states have received our options paper with interest. although not all doubts have been resolved and several member states have maintained their opposition in principle to this proposal, they are ready to study the issue further and the work will continue over the next few weeks at both experts meetings level and in the article 133 committee. i sincerely hope this will clear the way for a compromise solution. as honourable members know, the new article 207 of the treaty of lisbon gives parliament new and increased authority on legislative measures in the field of trade policy – and the ‘made in’ regulation could be one of the first to appear on honourable members’ desks. i am therefore very interested in keeping you closely involved in the further discussions on this important subject, and look forward to our brief debate now.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i shall be speaking on the european crime prevention network. this network was established in 2001 by council decision 2001/427/jha. the objectives of this network were to facilitate cooperation and the exchange of information and experience at national and european level, to collect and analyse relevant information, particularly for the purpose of exchanging best practice, to organise conferences, seminars, meetings and initiatives aimed at encouraging the exchange of experience and best practice, and also to provide advice to the council and the commission on crime prevention. the decision provided that the structure would be based on contact points designated by the commission and the member states, which should include at least one representative of the national authorities, while the other contact points could be designated from among researchers or specialised university teachers. however, member states were required to involve researchers, academics, ngos and civil society. even europol and the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction were involved as competent bodies. in 2005, the network underwent its first internal structural reform, which consistently provided for two committees one on the work programme and one on research while the management of the website was transferred from the european commission to the united kingdom, which still maintains it. in 2007 there was another review, which established the need to strengthen the secretariat first, also highlighting the need to address the issue of resources for standing committees and national representatives. in march 2009, an external evaluation of the operation of the network was published, which highlighted the importance of the objectives with which the network was created and, unfortunately, highlighted the organizational failure that prevented the achievement of the important objectives mentioned above. among the problems highlighted, which have led to the virtual collapse of the network, were the lack of appropriate resources, an ineffective secretariat, a lack of commitment from national representatives and a very poor work programme. the evaluation also considered the possibility of dismantling the network. it therefore set up a working group to examine the recommendations made in march 2009 and considered that amendments to the networking act were necessary. in particular, an external secretariat financed from the funds of community programmes was proposed. although some member states have raised the idea of dismantling the network, others have proposed reforming it. the swedish presidency of the council of the european union has taken up this proposal to the extent that it has become a priority in its six-month term of office. at this point i can only emphasize my personal embarrassment at seeing these empty seats, since it was the swedish presidency that had made these proposals its own. the proposal provides for the network to be composed of a secretariat, contact points designated by each member state and an administrative board. this board should be composed of national representatives appointed by the member states and chaired by a chairman who heads an executive committee. i think there is also a kind of confusion in this respect between the contact points and the national representatives. they are, by the way - and this is a very serious matter - completely cut off from the involvement of the world of civil society, the academic world, the world of experience and therefore the experts. the structural links between the network and the other community institutions and bodies dealing with crime and crime prevention are being completely cut. the decision does not provide for any form of cooperation with the european parliament and omits the requirement of knowledge of languages, which had been previously required. as rapporteur, i believe that this proposal is totally inefficient and is not able to tackle crime prevention for a number of reasons. first, it has not been able to achieve the objectives for which it was set up; secondly, there has been no cooperation between the commission, the council and the member states, and i think this is to be seen as a kind of sabotage of the network itself. crime prevention cannot be reduced to the exchange of best practices. unfortunately, we have witnessed almost a form of tourism of various officials going to the various countries on a visit and often not even being able to talk to each other because there was no form of translation. the lack of involvement of civil society and ngos, and the lack of development of prevention materials such as school papers, make this network totally inefficient. i believe that the network's powers should be strengthened to make it work, including the fight against crime and the prevention of organised crime. i therefore propose that the proposal be rejected, which could have been accepted only if the council had put forward a really ambitious proposal, which unfortunately did not come through.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with regard to the request to the council for approval of the draft exchange of information between europol and its partners, including third countries, the following is noted: the draft, if approved, would create the absurd situation of regulating, among other things, the exchange of information between europol and third countries, without parliament having yet approved the list of those countries. the draft, in describing the processing of personal data, seems to foreshadow the creation of a genuine unlimited database, which could even be available to third parties not yet defined by parliament. the council's draft states in article 15 (2) that in cases of absolute necessity, even beyond the possibility of a crime, data may be transmitted which reveal racial origin, ethnic origin, political opinions, religious and philosophical convictions, trade union membership, etc., without specifying what is meant by absolute necessity and, even worse, endorsing the idea that races exist. it would be interesting if the council clarified what a race is and what races are. as far as i am concerned, i believe that there is only one race of human beings, and that is the human race. for these reasons, but also to assert the autonomy of parliament, which must act within the time limit, i believe that the council's draft, under the present conditions, can only be rejected within the required deadline of 30 november.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the very interesting debate this evening has given us some very important insights, particularly on the european crime prevention network. firstly, with the lisbon treaty, parliament's role in the codecision procedure must be increasingly important, and this in two directions. the first is culture: the first thing that organised crime and the mafia do is to defeat each other with information and culture. a great italian magistrate, giovanni falcone, who was killed by the mafia, said that the mafia is a phenomenon that has a beginning and also an end. the end must be a great cultural mobilization, which must also start from europe and from parliament. a second point is that organized crime must be tackled more effectively, first of all by the creation of a european public prosecutor, and i think also by the introduction of certain very serious crimes, which are only provided for in certain member states of the union. i am referring, for example, to mafia crimes. we must understand that the mafia emergency is a european emergency, because the mafia has the capacity to penetrate very deeply into the institutions. there is a very close link between the mafia and corruption, as has been stated in recent reports, and fraud against the european union, as the court of auditors has also recently told us.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as shadow rapporteur on one of the europol dossiers, i can only repeat what has already been said by my predecessors. europol, through its functions of gathering, analysing and exchanging information, facilitates investigations in the member states, thus becoming an important tool in the fight against crime. if we are to be more effective in the fight against crime, we must also make a strong demand for the powers of this parliament. the council decided that it would adopt the europol package texts on 30 november, without waiting for the european parliament to obtain codecision on the matter with the entry into force of the lisbon treaty on 1 december. the rejection of the proposals is not intended to block the entry into operation of europol as a new european body, but to recognise that this parliament, the european parliament, has extended its powers, especially on important issues relating to the area of freedom, security and justice. finally, i think it is right to give parliament greater control over europol's activities to ensure that the processing of data held by europol's services does not infringe the rights of european citizens.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank the members who took part in the debate and, above all, i would like to thank commissioner barrot for sharing our concerns. our rejection proposals are not unjustified, they do not want to be a simple 'no' to the council. we would like to take part, because the treaty of lisbon will enter into force in a few days' time, and i believe that the co-decision role of this parliament is fundamental. i personally asked the council to present, immediately after the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, a proposal which was much more ambitious than the european crime prevention network. this proposal did not come. it is therefore absolutely necessary and obligatory to reject the proposal and i believe that parliament has the right to act in full co-decision, especially on such important issues. i thank mr nicholson for what he said about the role of the victims and the role of the executioners, roles which have too often been reversed. in the few months i have been in the european parliament, i have seen how the european parliament and the european union have attached extraordinary importance to the fight against terrorism, while unfortunately the will to tackle not only the fight against crime but also the organized crime that is at the root of crime is lacking. we cannot imagine fighting or preventing crime without assuming a more complex task of repression and prevention than organized crime and the mafia, as mr de magistris has reminded us by quoting the extraordinary words of judge falcone, who was killed by the mafia. with that said, i'd like to make a very small step as someone who unfortunately has had this experience on their own. too often, not only is there confusion between victim and executioner, but there are governments - and unfortunately the italian state does not pay much attention to this - that put on the agenda different types of victims of the same crime. victims of terrorism are treated one way, victims of the mafia another. i believe that these differences and discriminations cannot continue to exist, because in a europe which wants to base its policy on innovation, these differences cannot be tolerated.
in writing. the lisbon treaty significantly shifts the institutional balances established by the maastricht treaty in the area of judicial and police cooperation in criminal matters, introducing, with important exceptions, the ordinary legislative procedure for the area of freedom, security and justice. it is therefore necessary that any amendments to the measures implementing the europol decision be adopted within the framework of the new regulatory framework provided for by lisbon. europol cannot be strengthened without this parliament being able to express itself adequately on regulations which do not concern purely technical enforcement measures but political ones, such as the transfer of personal data. let me add to this a reflection on the union's growing external profile and the intensification of the synergy between internal security and defence. although the treaty will not have immediate consequences on the development of security and defence markets, it envisages the development of a more integrated and cohesive security market, which requires coordinated legislative action and thus interinstitutional action. it would therefore be all the more inconsistent, if not harmful, to adopt 'political' amendments to the provisions implementing the europol decision without following the regulatory process laid down by lisbon.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we will of course respect your decisions, but i believe that we have heard that you have made a reservation about certain amendments which are not directly related to the lisbon treaty. i may be wrong, but it seems to me that the committee on constitutional affairs has already had a general power to make proposals for regulatory changes throughout its history. it can do so if it is suggested by a group of members or by individual members and it can also do so on its own initiative. the fact that, in the context of a wider reform of the regulation, in accordance with the treaty of lisbon, it has taken the opportunity to make some corrections also in other respects does not seem to me to be something that can be considered unacceptable, especially since many amendments are suitable for transferring the spirit of lisbon into the regulation, sometimes through rules which are technically and materially reproduced in the regulation, but much more often by referring to the spirit of the treaty. it is enough to think of the role of parliament, which is strengthened in relation to the council but which is also strengthened by the regulation as regards internal relations with the institutions within parliament itself. of course, mr president, we will respect your decisions, but i felt it was my duty to make these remarks.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, by approving the martin report, the european parliament is fulfilling an inescapable task in view of the imminent entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, and it is doing so with a precise and accurate text which accurately incorporates into our rules of procedure the important innovations introduced by a new treaty as regards the increased role of the european parliament in the legislative, budgetary and more general institutional balance of the union. among these innovations i would like to mention those relating to the procedures for revising the treaties and the proactive role of parliament, as well as those relating to the role of the national parliaments which give the european parliament a special responsibility in terms of its ability to make this increased role a source of further democratic legitimacy for the construction of europe, rather than a bureaucratic obstacle. the president's decision to deal with the question of amendments not directly related to the task assigned to this report is a positive one, because there will then be time to examine the question of a more comprehensive revision of our rules of procedure in a more systematic and more systematic way. this does not mean that, while there are elements which can be eliminated in relation to the work done in the committee on constitutional affairs, there are others which can be usefully added. i refer to the importance of the amendment which stresses that the question of observers must be dealt with in the light of the fact that these observers must be chosen from among the candidates for the elections to the european parliament who are among the first of the non-elected.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there is certainly a real change in the nature of our institutions, of the european institutions. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very important one. that is why i believe that what is really at stake is, paradoxically, a strengthening of the federal dimension as well as the subsidiary dimension of the european union. this is a decisive fact for our future, all the more so since at this stage we have not sufficiently taken into account the figure of the citizen as a person, that is, as the centre and the end of political action. i want to explain. the level of harmonization we have achieved is satisfactory, and europe plays a major role in the lives of our citizens. however, instead of putting the individual, the family and intermediate groups at the centre of policy, the european union and the member states have often used subsidiarity to promote the interests of the institutions. the protection of the principle of subsidiarity, as expressed in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, is therefore more crucial than ever. we need a monitoring system to ensure that the legislative proposals submitted to parliament are really evaluated, especially as regards respect for the principle of subsidiarity, which is the starting point for institutions that are guarantors and not masters of the lives of citizens.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are putting a pitiful veil over the incredible sum of 30 billion euros per year until 2020 that the union would commit to allocate to emerging countries, essentially a lost cause. we italians are reminded of the infamous cassa del mezzogiorno. our amendments deal with three points. first, we are calling for legally binding and equally ambitious commitments, not only for the other industrialized countries, but also for the emerging economies, first of all china, india and brazil. secondly, we ask that any european funds which these countries may receive be made conditional on the use of technology 'made in the european union', so that our companies can at least partially be reimbursed for the additional and heavy emission reduction commitments which the union requires them to bear at their own expense. thirdly, we ask that the invention of innovative financial mechanisms not be used to create new financial speculation - for example, derivatives on the ets, or debt-for-nature swaps - which is a relic of the very serious crisis from which we have not yet emerged. that is why, if our amendments are rejected, our delegation - the northern league delegation - will vote against this resolution.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, minister carlgren, commissioner dimas, this morning i would like to speak about an 84-year-old missionary, father ettore turrini, who has already spent 59 years in the north-west of the amazon. he has always fought to defend the indians and their forests against those who would destroy them for short-term gain. to shoot in the forest father ettore had seven plane crashes, but he went ahead and collected tens of thousands of signatures for this activity, which he will submit to president lula, many ministers and the president of the napolitano republic. he was relentless. we met last sunday and i told him that i fully share his position, but that perhaps the world is waking up and coming to the conclusion that these forests are essential as the lungs of the world, for the local climate and also for the capture and sequestering of carbon. i told him that in copenhagen we would also find the resources to compensate those countries which respect the forests in their integrity. i told him that we're developing gps and inspire tracking tools to measure how governments are doing, and that by 2030, we're going to stop deforestation. in copenhagen we will be able to do all this and i will also be attending the summit for father turrini.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, in a few weeks i shall have the honour of being part of the official delegation that this parliament will send to copenhagen for the united nations conference on climate change. after the milestones of rio de janeiro in 1992 and kyoto in 1997, a new global climate conference, which could prove to be of historic importance, will begin on 7 december. i said 'may', madam president, because in the last days of the apec summit, the united states and china seem to have decided to reduce the scope of the copenhagen meeting. but there is still time before the summit, and it is in the interest of all actors to get there with concrete goals and programmes, so as not to disappoint the great expectations of making another step forward in the fight against climate change. the polluter pays principle must apply to all. europe has always been a leader and the climate and energy package of the last legislature is a clear example of this. we've said it many times before: the usa, china, india, russia and brazil also have to take responsibility as the biggest polluters. if this does not happen, we will be burdening our european companies with unnecessary costs and, above all, without the contribution of these countries, copenhagen too would risk being a missed opportunity. in conclusion, tackling climate change is also a necessary requirement towards achieving - or perhaps i should say approaching - the millennium development goals. we need to combat desertification, climate change and violent natural phenomena if we are to halve extreme poverty, fight epidemics and ensure that everyone has access to water, which is essential.

president of the commission. − mr president, there was this concrete issue on swift and i want to clarify the position on that matter because i think it is extremely important. it also has to do with the stockholm programme. the swift programme is, indeed, a very valuable instrument for member states in their fight against terrorism. it has allowed member states’ authorities to prevent terrorist attacks in europe. we are not talking about theoretical cases. we are talking about actual cases. the draft european union-united states agreement, which is currently being discussed, is an interim arrangement with a maximum duration of 12 months. it is needed in order to legally replace the existing one after the move of the data storage out of the united states. if the interim agreement is adopted before 1 december and the legal basis is changed, it will avoid a security gap and a serious blow to european union-united states relations in this area. in the recent meeting we had, involving the european union and president obama, the first issue he raised was the cooperation on the fight against terrorism between the united states and europe. he gave us the names of concrete countries in europe that escaped terrorist attacks recently because of the cooperation in this matter between us and them. i can give you some data on that, if you wish. more than 5 450 cases under the terrorist finance tracking programme have been passed to date to european governments, with over 100 new generated leads provided to european countries from january to september this year. i can give you concrete examples. this information has provided substantial assistance to european governments during the investigation into the al-qa’ida-directed plot to attack transatlantic airline flights travelling between the uk and the united states. in mid-september 2009 three individuals were convicted, and each was sentenced to at least 30 years in prison. in early 2009 this system was used to identify the financial activity of a europe-based al-qa’ida individual who played a role in the planning of an alleged attack on aircraft. the information was passed to the governments of european and middle eastern nations. in summer 2007 the same system was used to identify the financial activities of germany-based members of the islamic jihad union. this information contributed to mr president, in the light of the recent cases of suspension and revocation of the licence of many airlines, a considerable number of passengers and holders of unpaid and unreimbursed travel tickets have suffered considerable damage. i therefore believe that it is necessary to propose concrete legislation defining the most appropriate solutions to the problems arising from bankruptcies in terms of both economic loss and repatriation. it is therefore important to provide for compensation for passengers in the event of bankruptcy and to define the financial and administrative arrangements for this. i am referring to the principle of mutual responsibility for the protection of passengers of all airlines flying on the same route and having available seats. this would allow for the repatriation of passengers stranded at foreign airports. in this sense, the assumptions of a guarantee fund or compulsory insurance for airlines could represent plausible solutions to be balanced against the trade-off resulting from the increase in prices for final consumers.
mr president, the debate on designations of origin is not at all the overriding interest of one or a few member states, as is sometimes misunderstood, but embodies the fundamental economic principle of 'leveling the playing field'. this principle, in line with the lisbon treaty, aims to implement european competitiveness at world level by promoting clear and balanced rules for our companies producing and importing products from third countries. so we are talking about a matter which concerns europe as a whole. that is why i believe it is essential to have an agreement on designations of origin which goes beyond the interests of individual countries or political groups and leaves room for the will to implement the single market by promoting competitiveness and transparency. the proposal for a regulation on indication of origin, as formulated by the european commission in 2005, is now back in parliament. in this way, in line with the lisbon treaty, the codecision process between parliament and the council will make it possible to speed up the adoption of a regulation of such great importance for the european economy and consumers.

in writing. - finally, this resolution states important principles: the european union has a common responsibility in combating illegal immigration, in distributing asylum seekers, in returning foreign prisoners. i think it is very lacking and too complacent in the part where it calls for respect for the rights of minorities, and in particular the roma minority. the text completely ignores the degraded situation in which the roma communities in some countries, such as italy, are living, not because of a lack of integration policies, but because of a clear choice to reject all rules of civil life. no convictions for illegal activities (theft, pickpocketing, harassing begging, child prostitution) increasingly associated with the abusive settlements of roma in the suburbs of large cities, italian but not only. there is no mention, even in the section on the protection of minors, of the need to protect children from the slavery perpetrated against them by some roma family heads. nor is there any mention of how to implement the ec directive 2004/38 on the expulsion of community citizens who, after three months in an eu country, are unable to prove that they have a certain income. integration cannot exist without respect for the rules, and roma minorities are not exempt from respect for this principle.
